families.s: HSE safety signs, signals and workplace markings guidance
families.t: use, maintenance and interpretation of safety signs, signals and road markings where residual significant risk remains
f: Employers must provide safety signs where a significant risk remains after other relevant controls have been applied.
Safety signs are not required where they do not help reduce risk or the risk is not significant.
Provided safety signs must be maintained and unfamiliar signs must be explained to employees.
Safety signs and signals should be clear and legible and identify prohibitions, mandatory safeguards, warnings, fire equipment, exits or first-aid equipment.
Using too many signs can create confusion and should be avoided.
Private-workplace road signs should match public-road signs wherever a suitable sign exists.
Signs should be positioned so drivers and pedestrians have time to understand them and act before reaching the hazard.
Road markings can identify lanes, route edges, priorities, stop lines, crossings and no-parking areas.
families.g: Safety-sign effectiveness depends on the residual hazard, sign selection and positioning, visibility, maintenance, workforce understanding, traffic layout and whether stronger controls are already practicable.

families.s: HSE compressed-air systems and compressed-air work guidance
families.t: overpressure, bodily injection, plant integrity, decompression, competence, inspection and emergency controls
f: Compressed-air hazards include bodily entry through an orifice, skin penetration, explosions and eye injury from projected particles.
Overpressurisation can result from blockages, control failure, overspeeding, nearby fire, overheating or deposit accumulation.
Compressed-air safety management covers compressors, receivers, dryers, coolers, distribution systems, actuators and portable pneumatic equipment.
Inspection, maintenance and training are central controls for compressed-air plant.
The Work in Compressed Air Regulations require safe systems of work, competent people, suitable plant and equipment and health surveillance.
Compressed-air construction work requires controlled compression and decompression procedures, emergency arrangements and fire precautions.
Working in compressed air can cause decompression sickness, barotrauma and dysbaric osteonecrosis.
A contract medical adviser is required to provide occupational-health advice for work covered by the compressed-air regulations.
families.g: Compressed-air risk depends on operating pressure, plant design and condition, stored energy, tool and hose use, work environment, decompression profile, inspection results and worker competence.

families.s: HSE power-press safeguarding, inspection and examination guidance
families.t: safe use, guarding, daily testing, maintenance, thorough examination, competence and records for power presses
f: HSE guidance applies PUWER requirements to power presses working on cold metal.
Power-press precautions include safe use, safeguard inspection and thorough examination.
Power-press examination and inspection reports and related information must be retained as required.
Power-press maintenance should follow a structured system addressing who, what, when, why and how.
Thorough examination and testing must be carried out by a competent person.
Daily inspections and periodic maintenance should be documented using suitable records or checklists.
Power presses and their safeguards require examination before first use and periodically afterwards.
Guards and protection devices on power presses require frequent competent inspection and testing.
families.g: Power-press risk depends on press type and control system, tooling, guard design, safeguard condition, maintenance, examination interval, material handling and operator competence.

families.s: HSE abrasive-wheel selection, mounting, guarding and training guidance
families.t: wheel characteristics, mounting, machine operation, guards, portable grinders, training and protective equipment
f: Abrasive-wheel safety is managed under PUWER following repeal of the former Abrasive Wheels Regulations.
Wheel characteristics must be matched to the machine and intended grinding operation.
Safe wheel mounting procedures are necessary to reduce wheel failure risk.
Grinding machines require suitable guards.
Portable and hand-held grinders require additional task-specific precautions.
Suitable personal protective equipment is required for residual abrasive-wheel hazards.
People who mount or use abrasive wheels need appropriate training.
Maintenance of abrasive-wheel equipment should be performed by competent people with sufficient information and training.
families.g: Abrasive-wheel risk depends on wheel specification and condition, rotational speed, mounting, guard position, workpiece support, sparks and fragments, maintenance and user competence.

families.s: HSE chainsaw-at-work operation, competence and PPE guidance
families.t: competence, fitness, maintenance, protective clothing, first aid, lone work, felling and off-ground chainsaw use
f: Chainsaws can cause fatal or major injury when they are not used correctly.
Anyone using a chainsaw at work must receive adequate training and be competent for the type of work undertaken.
Chainsaw operators are required to wear appropriate protective clothing.
Risk control should consider the operator's fitness to use a chainsaw.
Chainsaws must be selected and maintained for the intended work.
Planning should address lone working and first-aid arrangements.
Tree felling and off-ground chainsaw work require additional safe-working controls.
Task assessment may require head, hearing, eye, leg, foot and other protection for chainsaw work.
families.g: Chainsaw risk depends on saw type and condition, task and timber, kickback potential, terrain and weather, work position, PPE, emergency arrangements and operator competence.

families.s: HSE agricultural-machinery safe-use and guarding guidance
families.t: safe stop, guarding, PTOs, blockages, maintenance, machine-specific hazards, design and competent use
f: Agricultural machines contain moving parts capable of causing serious or fatal injury.
Safe-stop procedures should be applied before leaving controls or approaching dangerous parts.
Operators must be competent for the machine and job.
Baler, harvester, mower, loader and cultivator hazards differ and require machine-specific controls.
PTO shafts and other transmission parts require suitable guarding.
Maintenance and blockage clearing are high-risk activities requiring machinery to be made safe.
New and second-hand machinery should be assessed for safe design and condition.
Mobile and stationary agricultural machinery require planned safe-working practices.
families.g: Agricultural-machinery risk depends on machine type, guards and interlocks, PTO condition, crop and blockage, terrain, maintenance state, safe-stop discipline and operator competence.

families.s: HSE pesticide selection, storage, transport, application and disposal guidance
families.t: integrated decision-making, risk assessment, competence, exposure control, storage, transport, application and disposal
f: The decision to use a pesticide should form part of a thorough risk assessment.
Pesticide use should be part of an integrated approach rather than an automatic first option.
Pesticide placing on the market, storage, use and disposal are strictly controlled.
Pesticides may be hazardous substances subject to COSHH controls.
Users should follow safe guidance for storage, transport, handling, application and disposal.
Pesticides can cause serious skin and respiratory harm.
People applying pesticides at work must be trained and competent for the task.
Weather conditions and suitable protective equipment must be considered when planning pesticide application.
families.g: Pesticide risk depends on product authorisation and formulation, concentration, application method, weather, exposure route, competence, PPE, storage, transport and disposal arrangements.

families.s: HSE natural-rubber-latex allergy and glove-selection guidance
families.t: sensitisation, asthma, dermatitis, anaphylaxis, glove selection, powder control, surveillance and workplace adjustment
f: Natural-rubber-latex proteins can cause asthma and dermatitis.
Latex exposure can rarely cause severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis.
Latex proteins can cause allergy through skin contact or inhalation of powder from powdered gloves.
Once sensitised, further low-level exposure can trigger symptoms.
Powdered latex gloves can disperse allergen-bearing powder into the air.
Powder-free low-protein latex gloves reduce allergy and latex-induced asthma risk compared with powdered gloves.
Employers must assess whether gloves are required and whether a non-latex alternative is more suitable.
Glove policies, employee information and appropriate skin or respiratory health surveillance may be required.
families.g: Latex-allergy risk depends on latex protein content, powder, frequency and route of exposure, individual sensitisation, glove policy, substitutes, ventilation and surveillance findings.

families.s: HSE occupational-asthma prevention and health-surveillance guidance
families.t: respiratory sensitisers, exposure prevention, control, surveillance, reporting and early intervention
f: Occupational asthma can result from allergic sensitisation to workplace respiratory sensitisers or asthmagens.
Once airways become hypersensitive, even low subsequent exposure can trigger an asthma attack.
Work-related asthma also includes pre-existing asthma aggravated by workplace irritants.
Isocyanates and flour are among the commonly reported causes of occupational asthma.
COSHH requires employers to control exposure to substances that can cause occupational asthma.
A prevention programme may require information, worker involvement and occupational-health support.
Prevention follows assessment, exposure prevention where practicable, adequate control, monitoring, surveillance and training.
Cases and relevant health findings may require reporting and review of controls.
families.g: Occupational-asthma risk depends on the sensitiser or irritant, airborne concentration, exposure duration, controls, individual susceptibility, latency, health surveillance and diagnostic evidence.

families.s: HSE manufactured-nanomaterial and high-aspect-ratio nanomaterial guidance
families.t: COSHH assessment and control for manufactured nanomaterials, carbon nanotubes and bio-persistent HARNs
f: HSE guidance addresses occupational exposure to manufactured nanomaterials.
COSHH applies to work with manufactured nanomaterials.
The guidance covers manufacture and manipulation of nanomaterials.
Carbon nanotubes and other bio-persistent high-aspect-ratio nanomaterials require specific attention.
Control principles can be applied across manufactured nanomaterials while accounting for material-specific differences.
Emerging toxicity evidence is relevant to the choice of precautionary controls.
Complex nanomaterial-control decisions may require competent professional advice.
Employee and trade-union safety representatives can use the guidance to support exposure control.
families.g: Nanomaterial risk depends on particle composition and morphology, size distribution, persistence, dustiness, process energy, exposure route, containment and measurement uncertainty.
